This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. Compared to traditional static count data models, the time-varying TV-PARX model delivers significantly more accurate forecasts and provides a robust framework for real-time inference about the underlying data-generating process. The source code for the R package 'scorecount' is available at https://github.com/mahmoudhammoud89/ScoreCount.

Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. This paper provides an updated overview of this technique, detailing efforts to enhance measurement accuracy and its emerging applications. We present a forward model of the technique that incorporates recent refinements, which are summarized alongside discussions of past limitations and future directions. Notably, the method has been utilized to assess the impact of volcanic plumes following the eruption of Indonesia's Kawah Ijen volcano and to quantify aerosol changes in the upper atmosphere due to satellite launches. Looking ahead, the technique will be further employed to evaluate the atmospheric entry of meteorites and the re-entry of orbital vehicles. Furthermore, there are ongoing plans to use this method for verifying the calibration of the new SHARAD instrument on the Japanese BEXUS-29 stratospheric balloon mission. Finally, we briefly explore the potential of applying this method extraterrestrially to measure the atmospheric circulation of exoplanets. Complementary techniques for validating VAOD, such as Raman scattering, are also discussed, and we provide an updated summary of recent VAOD measurements obtained via stellar photometry.

Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02407, elaborating on key technical aspects and deriving further consequences. Specifically, we provide a complete solution to the state complexity problem for a specific family of primary states defined by constant energy-momentum expectations, termed "primary states." Similarly, we fully address the operator complexity issue for a corresponding set of primary transformations. Our results demonstrate that primary states, when defined via their constant energy-momentum expectations, constitute the most accessible states. Furthermore, we establish a generalized triangle inequality for complexity, confirming that complexity functions satisfy all axioms required of a metric. These findings align with existing literature on quantum complexity, although our specific measure differs because it is defined directly in terms of primary field theories through a geodesic distance on the space of states and transformations. As a significant application, we derive an upper bound for the complexity of thermal states of a free real scalar field, expressed as $\mathcal{C}(\rho_{\beta})\leq\frac{\pi}{6}\coth\left(\frac{\pi\mu}{6}\right)\beta$, where $\beta$ represents the inverse temperature and $\mu$ denotes the Mazur bound of our state complexity metric. Notably, this bound diverges as the temperature approaches zero ($\beta\to\infty$), a divergence that arises specifically from the definition of our metric via a geodesic distance along primary field theory gradients. In contrast, standard metrics on quantum states, such as the Fubini-Study metric, remain finite for thermal states even under this geodesic definition. Ultimately, our framework paves the way for defining complexity among primary states and transformations in other field theories through their respective conformal primaries.

This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements of this framework, two triplets of neutral particles and two triplets of charged particles must exist. Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF provider must incorporate DGLAP evolution. This paper details how all these elements were consolidated into a single C++ based provider, known as TPIP (Parton Distribution Function Provider for Tau-X Fitting), which connects directly to the fitting engine. We demonstrate its efficacy by fitting CT18 and ABM18 distributions against the Tau-X dataset. Additionally, we present a standalone source code package designed to generate an XML file defining process parameters for any specific process, facilitating rapid implementation of new processes into the provider. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/CTEQ-Tableski理论/TFPIP-Providier. We are confident that this pipeline will accelerate the development of future PDF sets. While initially created for the Tau-X fitting project, the provider supports any process included in MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, up to two loops, provided that runcards and matrix element libraries are available. Distributions can also be evaluated at any scale by specifying the momentum transfer in the "Q" parameter within the runcard. Finally, this project can be easily extended to other processes with known NLO predictions, such as total cross sections.

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Furthermore, the linearized framework was utilized to examine the influence of global Strouhal number, Mach number, and Reynolds number on reaction rate fluctuations, with results discussed in detail. Finally, this study provides a comprehensive characterization of low-order modes of reaction rate fluctuations, highlighting the dominance of the first mode (K-H mode) at low Strouhal numbers and the emergence of higher-order modes at elevated Strouhal numbers. These low-order modes of reaction rate and velocity fluctuations excited by upstream acoustic disturbances could serve as a foundation for developing reduced-order models in control applications aimed at flame noise suppression. The investigated framework and approach hold significant potential for analyzing reaction rate fluctuations under various fluctuation sources, such as vortex-induced fluctuations or those caused by transverse oscillations.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when a modified constitutive relation for NLG is applied to derive the field equations of a generalized Palatini f(R) theory (where f(R) need not be linear), an additional term emerges on the right-hand side of these equations. This finding suggests that NLG and nonlocal f(R) gravity are distinct theoretical frameworks. The study concludes by proposing a constitutive relation for NLG that could facilitate the derivation of Einstein-Aether field equations.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. These findings support the conclusion that neutron star LMXBs are inherently rarer than black hole LMXBs and that non-outbursting systems represent the majority of the neutron star LMXB population.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Additionally, for the practical range where $k \le 10$, we provide a heuristic algorithm. Evaluated on real-world data, this approach successfully generated planar bipartite graphs for seven networks previously unsuccessful with standard embedding techniques, including two significant academic networks totaling 109,000 edges. The source code and datasets required to replicate our results are accessible at https://github.com/tian-ruobing/BiSplit. Our findings indicate that this new method effectively reduces complexity and produces high-quality plans for sparse graphs, performing notably better than existing approaches on real-world datasets. Specifically, it generated planar representations for seven large-scale bipartite graphs for which no planar embedding had been possible beforehand. A video demonstrating this method is available at https://youtu.be/00vX7s0s2t0. We define the necessary graph theory terminology, presenting a planar bipartite graph as a bipartite graph admitted by at least one planar drawing. In such a drawing $\mathcal{D}$, we distinguish between "original" edges, which do not intersect vertices other than their endpoints, and "crossing" edges, which intersect at least one vertex besides their endpoints. We establish that minimizing crossings in $\mathcal{D}$ is equivalent to minimizing them between the pairs of edges involved. Furthermore, we prove that a bipartite graph can be made planar by splitting at most two vertices if and only if it is outerplanar. Finally, we show that determining whether a given bipartite graph requires splitting at least three vertices to become planar is NP-complete.

Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, we devised a countermeasure and validated its efficacy through experimental testing.

It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Our findings indicate that the distance measured by the diagonal move correlates strongly with other unknotting distance metrics for classical knots. Finally, we establish that the diagonal move serves as a valuable tool for studying unknotting processes in both classical and welded knots. Specifically, we prove that the Yokoyama invariant for welded knots and the Kauffman invariant for classical knots remain constant under the diagonal move in the context of classical knots.

This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. To validate the approach in a practical context, a hardware demonstration of NOVR-XL was constructed and tested against existing solutions, confirming the significant sum rate gains achieved by the proposed method.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. This hybrid approach enables the neural component to concentrate on deeper linguistic understanding while offering a flexible framework for customization; one can switch the underlying $N$-gram model without retraining the neural component. Experiments across three standard tasks—language modeling, machine translation, and summarization—consistently show that our method outperforms existing standalone neural models. Furthermore, the approach facilitates effective domain adaptation by simply swapping in a domain-specific $N$-gram model, requiring no additional training. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant influences of beta-plane gravity wave drag are observed at high rotation rates combined with strong thermal damping. Additionally, significant poleward jets develop when the Coriolis force and frictional forces are balanced, particularly when radiative time scales are short and frictional time scales are long. These jets form between the equator and the mid-latitudes as the planet's rotation rate increases from Eastward values of -0.5 to +0.5 relative to Earth. At the highest rotation rates, the balance shifts toward between the Coriolis force, friction, and inertial (centrifugal) forces; under these conditions, strong friction and low thermal gradients result in multiple western boundary currents and super-rotating zonal jets. These findings suggest that the planet's rotation rate, along with the relative strengths of frictional, Coriolis, and radiative time scales, primarily drives the formation of different atmospheric circulation regimes in Earth-like planets. This work represents significant outcomes of the EU-funded ATMOS/ATMOS-2 projects. This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. These contributions offer fresh perspectives on the definition of the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function and could support future investigations into its numerical computation. The proposed regularized forms are particularly valuable for analyzing the classical complex representations of both the $\Gamma$ and Bessel functions. Furthermore, the paper derives a novel regularized formula for the product of two Bessel functions and establishes its connection to a specific regularized complex integral involving the product of two Hankel functions. A table summarizing the various expressions of this product is included.

Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models by enabling simulations beyond the long-wavelength and low-Mach-number restrictions and by offering access to quantum fluctuations. In the context of a suddenly quenched superfluid transition, our simulations demonstrate that while mean-field predictions align well with post-quench dynamics up to a critical dimension $d_c = 2.7 \pm 0.3$, significant deviations occur at lower dimensions. Furthermore, the simulation results confirm that positive-P stochastic hydrodynamics remains valid even under extreme conditions, such as strong explosions following a black-hole-like Quasi-Normal-Mode oscillations. These findings indicate that this framework can explore quantum many-body dynamics under various non-equilibrium scenarios where different physical mechanisms are involved. Ultimately, positive-P stochastic hydrodynamics serves as a potent tool for investigating early-time post-quench many-body dynamics across diverse quantum phase transitions, including those in ultra-cold atomic systems, trapped ions, and circuit quantum electrodynamics. The implementation of this method is available as a standalone code at https://github.com/tommasoattard/positivePHydro and integrated into the Squid simulation platform.

We introduce a new, compact representation for graphical models, a foundational framework for numerous reasoning tasks. Leveraging deterministic finite state automata, we integrate this concise representation into Bucket Elimination (BE), a general variable elimination method used for inference and optimization problems like most probable explanation and constrained optimization. We refer to this enhanced approach as FABE. Incorporating our compact representation into FABE significantly enhances BE's performance regarding both runtime and memory usage. Empirical comparisons between FABE and leading methods for most probable explanation (recursive best-first, structured message passing) and constrained optimization (CPLEX, GUROBI, toulbar2), conducted via a standard methodology, validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating runtime gains of up to five orders of magnitude. Furthermore, we formally establish the equivalence between our deterministic automaton-based method and recent work by de Salve-Bouquet et al. ([AAAI] 2019), which utilizes nondeterministic automata, confirming that our deterministic version is at least as efficient as the nondeterministic one. Our implementation is accessible at: https://github.com/jeremyshay/FA-BD. These results imply that our method could serve as a powerful, general-purpose alternative to specialized algorithms for constrained optimization problems, potentially reducing the necessity for further research into dedicated solutions for specific constraint types. Keywords: probabilistic graphical models, finite state machines, most probable explanation, constrained optimization, bucket elimination.

The recently introduced higher rank Racah algebra $R(n)$ is reviewed, followed by the definition of a quotient algebra by central elements termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$. Leveraging classical invariant theory, it is demonstrated that $sR(n)$ is isomorphic to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ corresponding to the diagonal embedding of $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^{\otimes n}$. This isomorphism yields a new presentation of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ via generators and relations. Furthermore, an explicit Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is derived and analyzed, with the implications of these findings extended to the special Askey-Wilson algebra and its higher rank variants. Finally, a conjecture regarding the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of $R(n)$, special Racah algebras of other types, and their corresponding special higher rank Askey-Wilson algebras is presented. These special higher rank Racah and Askey-Wilson algebras represent a distinct family from the higher rank $q$-Racah and Askey-Wilson algebras (together with their related $q$-deformed Lie algebra centralizers), a difference that manifests clearly in their respective Hilbert-Poincar\'e series. The special higher rank Racah and Askey-Wilson algebras are defined over the commutative algebra $\mathbb{C}(u,v)$ of rational functions in two variables, a fact that significantly complicates numerical computations. Consequently, a strategy for addressing this challenge through a deformation of these algebras and their Hilbert-Poincar\'e series is proposed. These special higher rank Racah and Askey-Wilson alges constitute a subject of interest in mathematical physics, particularly in relation to centralizers of Lie algebra actions, invariant theory, and integrable models such as spin chains. From pure mathematics perspectives, they offer a promising arena for investigating open problems in commutative algebra, including unimodality and the Lewis-Small conjecture.

Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(GN (\log GN )(\log N ))$ time, where $N$ represents the dataset size and $G$ denotes the range of the test statistic. Experimental results indicate that our exact algorithm is 10 times faster than a Monte Carlo approximation using 20,000 samples on a standard dataset. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficiency scales effectively with both dataset size and the complexity of the test statistic. By enabling the rapid computation of precise p-values, this method allows linguists and computer scientists to reliably assess significant performance differences across system pairs without being constrained by the ability to generate large numbers of permutations for high-confidence p-values. The source code and data required to replicate our experiments are accessible at https://github.com/yzhang-kuu/ExactPairedPermutation.

Using the AMPT multiphase transport model, we investigated the connection between initial geometric anisotropy and anisotropic flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Our results show that, unlike the elliptic flow $v_2$, the triangular flow $v_3$ exhibits minimal dependence on centrality. Once the influence of initial geometry is accounted for, the ratio $v_3/\epsilon_3$ rises with increasing transverse particle density, mirroring the behavior of $v_2/\epsilon_2$. Furthermore, the $p_T$ dependence of $v_3$ observed across identified particles follows a qualitative pattern similar to that of $v_2$. These findings support the conclusion that collective flow driven by initial geometric anisotropy plays a significant role in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at this energy.

We derive an explicit description of both the spectral and orbital stability for solitary wave solutions to the one-dimensional $\mathbf{U}(1)$-invariant Klein--Gordon equation, which is coupled to an anharmonic oscillator. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the spectrum resulting from the linearization around these solitary waves. Our findings fill critical gaps in previous research regarding the spectral stability of bound states for Gaussian solitary waves connected to an anharmonic oscillator and confirm the orbital stability of certain first-pentamode bound states. Throughout this study, we refrain from utilizing a variational approach to establish inertial stability. Instead, we fully characterize the spectrum relative to the orthogonal complement of the generator of phase invariance, which corresponds to a zero eigenvalue with a Jordan block of size two. This complete characterization allows us to derive inertial stability conclusions without needing to verify the specific form of the eigenvalues.

At colliders, neutral long-lived particles are identified either via displaced decay products or as missing energy, with the optimal search strategy depending on both the detector characteristics and the particle's decay length. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through displaced vertex searches at Belle II, long-lived particle studies at the LHC, and future fixed-target experiments. As a initial estimate, integrating the limits predicted by this work with existing constraints, a branching ratio of $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) = 10^{-6}$ and couplings $g_{\gamma N} \sim 10^{-3}$ (where $g_{\gamma N} \equiv E_N f_B m_B / \Gamma_{B\to a})$ remain unexplored for masses $m_a < 0.27\,$GeV.

Expectation values of position were computed for different combinations of mass, natural angular frequency, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ under both driving conditions. Under constant forcing, the simulations yielded coherent states. The outcomes for both scenarios align almost perfectly with theoretical predictions. To perform these simulations, we implemented the Metropolis algorithm on a discrete time lattice to evaluate the systems' imaginary time path integrals. This meta-simulation serves as a numerical implementation of the Monte Carlo method. Under driven conditions, the path integrals reveal striking patterns of interference along the imaginary time dimension. These simulations demonstrate that path integral simulations are feasible for both simple and complex quantum systems, offering a valuable tool for investigating quantum phenomena, particularly when direct observation is difficult. Furthermore, these simulations provide an imaginary time path integral Monte Carlo simulation for a driven quantum harmonic oscillator, illustrating how such simulations can reveal quantum interference effects. Ultimately, this approach serves as a practical example of how path integral Monte Carlo methods can expose quantum behavior in similar systems. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. Ultimately, this research advocates for a more data-driven strategy when choosing a loss function for any given dataset.

Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on taxonomic information, ATOMIC emphasizes inferential knowledge formatted as typed if-then relations involving variables (for instance, "if X pays Y a compliment, then Y will likely return the compliment"). This work tackles novel view video prediction, where a network generates video from an unseen angle based on input clips from one or multiple existing views. Unlike recent methods that handle only minor viewpoint shifts, our prior-free approach successfully predicts videos across wider angular ranges, up to 45 degrees. Furthermore, the method utilizes solely RGB frames to learn a dual representation comprising both view-dependent and global components; the latter integrates complementary details to facilitate prediction from novel viewpoints. We validate the framework's efficacy on two real-world datasets, NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic. Comparative analysis against state-of-the-art techniques reveals significant improvements without relying on explicit priors from target views: a 26.1% gain in SSIM, a 13.6% increase in PSNR, and a 60% reduction in FVD scores. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/AnuragSrivastava98/NPV-DSR.

Fake news spreads rapidly across social media, reaching global audiences and endangering communities. While deep learning models perform well on labeled data for specific events, their efficacy often drops when encountering new events due to domain shifts. This creates a significant hurdle for existing detection systems when dealing with emergent events where large, labeled datasets are scarce. Furthermore, adapting to new events typically requires training a model from scratch or extensive fine-tuning, which is often costly, impractical, and difficult to sustain in real-world scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework designed to rapidly learn fake news detection for emerging events using only a small number of verified posts. By combining meta-learning with neural process methods, our approach leverages the strengths of both techniques. Specifically, we incorporate a label embedding module and a hard attention mechanism to better manage categorical data and filter out irrelevant content. Extensive experiments on multimedia datasets from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects fake news in previously unseen events, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The code for this project is available at: https://github.com/ST-UCSD/Multimodal_Emergent_Fake_News_Detection_Via_Meta_Learning.

Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. Furthermore, this recipe-based reconstruction framework is versatile and can be adapted to reconstruct various other damage mechanisms in self-sensing composites, such as cracks and impact-induced complex deformations, simply by updating the corresponding physics-based model. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/.

Discourse markers, such as {\it by contrast} and {\it happily}, are words or phrases that indicate semantic and/or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Using this dataset, we present initial statistical insights into the distribution of discourse markers across different discourse relation categories. Furthermore, demonstrating the practical utility of DiscSense, we trained a classifier to distinguish between directness and indirectness in illicit discourse relations leveraging this dataset and confirmed its efficacy with additional data. Finally, we sketched out a preliminary plan for creating a structured dataset linking discourse markers to relations, akin to lexitional resources like lexicons or grammatical metadata in dictionaries. To move in this direction, we extracted a dataset of potential marker-relations pairs from DiscSense and proposed using deep neural networks for classification. We outlined several tasks required to build such a resource and provided initial evidence for its feasibility. Our findings and proposals are intended to stimulate research into structurally organized datasets of discourse markers and their associated relations, similar to established lexitional resources. To support this goal, we open-sourced all models and datasets utilized in this study at \url{https://github.com/akhgrewal/DiscSense}.

We introduce an explicit extension of the $r$-symmetrized Jordanian twist originally formulated by Giaquinto and Zhang. We demonstrate that this generalization fulfills the 2-cocycle condition. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions for the associated star product and twisted coproduct. Finally, we establish that our generalized twist is equivalent to the simple Jordanian twist modified by a 1-cochain. This equivalence confirms that our extension constitutes a gauge transformation of the simple twist. These results expand the understanding of Lie group twists and their application in deformations of Hopf algebras to serve as Drinfel'd twists. Specifically, our finding aligns with the principle that, for semisimple Lie groups, no genuinely new twists exist beyond gauge transformations of the simple twist, a concept first highlighted by Reshetikhin for $SU(2)$.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, which incorporate intersection and complement operators, and for expressions defined over potentially infinite character sets. Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. The authors present a new symbolic decision procedure for containment, utilizing Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives alongside Antimirov's rewriting technique. Furthermore, they extend Brzozowski's syntactic derivative operator to handle comparisons between regular expressions and character sets (or words), even when those sets are specified set-comprehension style rather than by listing individual characters. The algorithm further incorporates context-free grammar matching rules to manage the complement operator. Demonstrations of practical application are provided through the analysis of wildcard regexes in software utility tools and the formulation of access control policies within database systems. Extensive experiments conducted with a prototype implementation of the method are also detailed. The source code for this article is accessible at https://github.com/huanghuab/SymbolicSolvingOfExtendedRegularExpressionInequalities.

Building upon the research of \cite{Ferrara:1971vh} and \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we derive an integral representation for OPE blocks associated with spinning primaries in CFT$_{2}$. We find that when these blocks are constructed from conserved spinning primaries, the integral decomposes into a product of two weighted AdS$_{2}$ field copies, smeared along geodesics. Consequently, conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_{2}$ admit a distinct formulation via AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators rather than the traditional AdS$_{3}$ geodesic operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this perspective connects to AdS$_{3}$ massless higher spin fields through HKLL bulk field reconstruction. Leveraging this framework, we successfully derive a closed-form expression for the four-point spinning conformal block as a product of two AdS$_{2}$ Geodesic Witten diagrams. This result aligns precisely with the factorization of AdS$_{3}$ geodesics into two half-geodesics.

We introduce the concept of multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics to substantially decrease the number of focal plane detectors required for wide-field X-ray monitors using lobster-eye (LE) technology. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment onto one image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When each LE segment is oriented at a distinct rotation angle, the azimuthal rotation of the reconstructed cross-like image from a point source allows for the identification of the specific segment responsible for focusing the X-rays onto the imager. Utilizing a 30 cm focal length and 10 x 10 cm^2 LE segments, a field of view covering approximately 1 steradian can be achieved with 36 segments and just four imagers (each with a total area of 10 x 10 cm^2). Ray tracing simulations were conducted to assess a nine-segment MuLE configuration. These simulations indicated that for a 100-second transient, the flux corresponding to a 5-sigma detection limit between 0.5 and 2 keV would be approximately 2 x 10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1 (10 mCrab). Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the direction of transients with fluxes ranging from 15 to 0.15 times this limit could be determined with 99.9% precision. We conclude that the MuLE configuration has significant potential as a cost-effective instrument for on-board wide-field X-ray monitors designed to identify and localize transients, thereby triggering multi-wavelength follow-up observations. This paper serves as the first in a series exploring the design, simulation, and simulation-based characterization of a demo MuLE instrument intended to complement the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) on the International Space Station.

Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. Within the region of maximum magnetic field concentration near the superconductor's surface, the magnetic field strength reaches approximately 100 nT, corresponding to a flux density of roughly 0.1 $\mu$T. At this level, the atomic wavefunction experiences significant splitting, which amplifies the atomic interferometer's phase shift beyond what would occur in the absence of the superconductor. By comparing the phase shifts with and without the superconductor present, we derive a simple formula for the maximum detectable field. Employing this method, we achieved a magnetic field sensitivity of 0.5 fT/$\sqrt{\text{s}}$ over an integration period of 20 s using an atomic fountain with a 2.5 m drop height. This sensitivity represents a factor of four improvement over the best sensitivity attainable with a standard SQUID operating under similar conditions. Ultimately, this demonstration highlights the potential of atomic interferometry for detection tasks that exceed the capabilities of conventional magnetometers, including applications in navigation, geophysics, and fundamental physics experiments. The experimental setup is straightforward, requires no modifications to existing atomic interferometry arrangements, and can be readily implemented in both laboratory and field environments. Furthermore, as this approach relies solely on local magnetic field measurements, it remains unaffected by gravitational wave disturbances, a limitation that plagues other methods like laser interferometers. Preliminary data suggest that with an integration time of one hour, a sensitivity of 0.1 fT could be achieved, potentially enabling the detection of gravitational wave-induced magnetic field fluctuations via this technique. Invariant manifolds constitute crucial sets within the stability analysis of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. These conclusions serve as essential prerequisites for extending invariant manifold theory to the realm of fractional-order dynamical systems. Finally, we summarize key applications related to stability investigation and bifurcation analysis in this context. Notably, these applications reveal that certain biological models of HIV infection, when formulated as fractional-order systems, exhibit a backward bifurcation where an additional positive equilibrium emerges via a transcritical bifurcation; however, this new equilibrium is unstable, and the system's dynamics are governed by an unstable invariant straight line. Consequently, the anticipated global asymptotic stability of the endemic equilibrium in fractional-order systems does not materialize, implying that control parameters must be adjusted to drive the virus concentration below undetectable levels. Control strategies are also examined under this framework. This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary interface. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate. These mathematical findings were validated by numerical experiments, which also demonstrated the method's ability to handle noisy data.

This study examines the dark matter (DM) phenomenology, vacuum stability properties, and parameter constraints within the simplest extension of the simplest Scoto-Seesaw (SS2) model. Unlike prior investigations that utilized a generic U(1) dark sector, we implement an explicit seesaw mechanism for the DM mass, rendering it a function of underlying parameters rather than a free variable. To achieve a stable electroweak vacuum, at least two heavy right-handed neutrinos ($N_R$) and one scalar singlet ($\eta$) must exist beyond the Standard Model. We demonstrate that achieving the observed DM mass ($\sim$1 GeV) requires significant fine-tuning, while simultaneously compromising vacuum stability. By relaxing the 1 GeV mass requirement, we map out the "dm-fertile" region, where the DM mass ranges from $\sim$1 to 100 GeV. In this range, less fine-tuning is needed, and the vacuum remains metastable. Our analysis indicates that for DM masses exceeding $\sim$10 MeV, direct detection experiments will likely constrain the parameter space, potentially ruling out this specific configuration. Furthermore, we observe that the simplest Scoto-Seesaw framework struggles to satisfy the direct detection limits imposed by XENON1T. Finally, we propose an extended variant of this model capable of meeting such experimental bounds. Our findings highlight that while the simplest Scoto-Seesaw model offers a theoretically consistent approach to WIMP dark matter, it faces substantial challenges in aligning with current direct detection data. Extending the scalar sector remains the most effective strategy for addressing these issues and accommodating a wider variety of DM masses. This work serves as a foundational step toward a complete phenomenological examination of this model's dark matter characteristics. Additionally, the detailed examination of DM properties in our study reveals a novel phenomenon: a transition in the dominant annihilation channel as the DM mass increases. Specifically, annihilation into muon pairs ($\mu^+\mu^-$) supersedes that into pion pairs ($\pi^+\pi^-$) around 10 MeV, while the channel involving $B$-mesons ($B\bar{B}$) becomes dominant near 2 GeV. These results are particularly relevant for experiments operating in the MeV scale, such as SHPPE, and could guide future investigations.
